findings.reason: a done-when clause that compares absent-to-absent cannot fail, so the node's gate would report success on the very assertion it was meant to prove.
findings.text: the first case requires that the re-dispatch keeps "its run id, manifest path, session and base", but `_queued_request_record` (reckon/crew/dispatch.py:205-252) writes no `base_sha` key and a live queued pointer carries none (observed keys on `r-20261027T092056010872-a-mention-is-charged-a-reference-cost`: no `base_sha`, no `session_id`, no `argv`); the new record has no base either, so the "keeps its ... base" clause passes whether or not the merge is implemented

findings.reason: the mechanism as written satisfies its own done-when while leaving the incident's failure (resume refused for a missing session id, landing refused for a missing argv) unaddressed, so a node would ship a fix that does not repair the defect it was dispatched for; the plan needs to say where those fields are written and which record the merge must carry them from.
findings.text: the Why section says the live pointer lost `session_id`, `argv` and `base_sha` and that `crew resume` and the landing pass then refused, but the deliverable's remedy is to keep the queued request's identity fields, and a queued request carries none of those three: `_queued_request_record` (dispatch.py:205-252) stores `session` (the coordinator session string, not the worker's `session_id`) and no `argv`/`base_sha` at all, so merging the existing request's fields back cannot restore them

findings.reason: the guard names the module that was dropped from the write paths rather than the module being edited, so a regression introduced in `runs.queue_dispatch` could pass the stated gate.
